title: Glucose and insulin
chapter: Diabetes: what happens inside the body?
text: Blood glucose is the concentration of glucose in blood. Digestion supplies glucose, and the liver also releases glucose between meals. Insulin from the pancreas reduces liver glucose production and helps muscle and fat cells take up glucose. Blood vessel damage is not caused by sticky sugar coating vessels. Prolonged high glucose and other metabolic and vascular factors contribute.

title: Type 1 and type 2 differ
chapter: Diabetes: what happens inside the body?
text: Type 1 usually involves autoimmune damage to insulin-producing cells and requires insulin treatment. It can begin in adulthood. Type 2 involves insulin resistance and impaired insulin secretion, influenced by genetics, age, body fat and living conditions. Other forms include gestational diabetes and diabetes related to pancreatic disease or medicines. This book focuses on adult prediabetes and type 2, not pregnancy or type 1 treatment.

title: Diagnosis is different from treatment targets
chapter: Diabetes: what happens inside the body?
text: Laboratory fasting glucose 100–125 mg/dL, 2-hour glucose 140–199 mg/dL after a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test, or HbA1c 5.7–6.4% are prediabetes ranges. Diabetes thresholds are 126, 200 and 6.5%, respectively. An oral glucose tolerance test is not an ordinary after-meal reading. Without unequivocal symptoms or a hyperglycemic crisis, confirmation is usually needed. Anemia and other conditions may affect HbA1c. A clinician interprets the findings together. Record whether the test was fasting, after a meal or an oral glucose tolerance test. An HbA1c below 7% is considered for many adults, but national guidance, age and hypoglycemia risk affect the target. A diagnostic threshold is not automatically your target.

title: Prediabetes is an opportunity to act
text: Prediabetes means glucose is above normal but below diabetes thresholds. Not everyone progresses to diabetes. Review blood pressure, lipids, smoking and daily circumstances as well as glucose.

title: Weight and activity goals
text: Adults at high risk with overweight or obesity can consider individualized weight loss of about 5–7% or more and work toward 150 minutes of moderate activity weekly. With normal weight, frailty or low muscle mass, preserving nutrition and muscle may take priority over weight loss. Choose one change this week: water instead of sugary drinks, or a ten-minute walk each day.

title: Follow-up and preventive medication
text: At least annual glucose assessment is recommended for prediabetes, with more frequent testing when risk or changes warrant it. Clinicians may consider metformin for selected high-risk people. Prediabetes does not mean everyone needs medication. Agree on the next test date and your weight and activity goals at your visit. Remission of type 2 is not a cure. It generally means HbA1c below 6.5% for at least three months without glucose-lowering medication; ongoing monitoring remains necessary.

title: Why prescriptions differ
text: Medication choice considers heart failure, cardiovascular and kidney disease, weight, hypoglycemia and cost as well as glucose. Certain SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 medicines have proven heart or kidney benefits in studied populations; those results cannot be assigned equally to every ingredient. Check ingredient names, strength and whether the formulation is extended-release.

title: Medicine class map
text: The table summarizes classes. Use the ingredient tool for ingredient-specific notes and combination cautions. A low hypoglycemia risk when used alone does not mean the same risk when combined with insulin or secretagogues.

title: Formulation, timing and sick days
text: The same ingredient may have different instructions as immediate-release, extended-release, injectable or oral formulations. Insulin action varies with ingredient, concentration and individual factors. Follow product-specific instructions for medicines such as oral semaglutide. Ask your pharmacist or clinician for missed-dose and fasting, surgery or vomiting plans in advance. Do not apply a blanket continue-or-stop rule when unable to eat or dehydrated. SGLT2 medicines and metformin may need situation-specific changes; stopping basal insulin without guidance in type 1 can be dangerous.

title: Start with a balanced meal
chapter: Food: what and how much to eat?
text: You do not have to remove all rice, noodles or bread. Combine nonstarchy vegetables, fish, tofu, beans or lean protein, and appropriate grain portions. The plate method is a starting tool, not a calculation of individual energy needs. For Korean meals, plan rice portions with fish or tofu and vegetable sides. For Vietnamese meals, consider noodle portions, sweet sauces and drinks together. Kidney disease, heart failure or digestive conditions may require changes to protein, sodium, potassium or fluids. More vegetables or water is not always better.

title: Carbohydrate quantity and quality
chapter: Food: what and how much to eat?
text: Whole grains, beans and whole fruit can be good choices, but large portions still raise glucose. Juice and sugary drinks make it easy to consume a lot of sugar. Prefer suitable portions of whole fruit; blending alone does not make every food forbidden. Read serving size, total carbohydrate and sugars together. Sugar-free does not necessarily mean carbohydrate-free.

title: Meal order is an optional supporting strategy
chapter: Food: what and how much to eat?
text: Some studies find smaller post-meal glucose excursions when vegetables and protein come before carbohydrate. This does not replace portion or food choices; long-term HbA1c effects must be distinguished from short-term glucose changes. Differences in participants and meals prevent a single promised percentage.

title: Fasting, low-carbohydrate diets and medicines
chapter: Food: what and how much to eat?
text: Several patterns, including Mediterranean-style eating and appropriate carbohydrate reduction, can fit individual preferences and goals. Insulin, sulfonylurea or meglitinide users must consider hypoglycemia when intake falls. Extreme carbohydrate restriction or prolonged fasting with SGLT2 medicines can increase ketoacidosis concerns. Agree on medication and monitoring plans before major dietary changes.

title: Review sleep and stress
text: Sleep duration, quality and regularity, and stress relate to appetite, activity and self-care. Loud snoring and daytime sleepiness warrant assessment for sleep apnea. Treatment does not guarantee improved glucose for everyone. Keep a regular wake time and choose sustainable relaxation such as comfortable breathing or a short walk.

title: Alcohol can cause delayed hypoglycemia
text: Alcohol can interfere with liver glucose supply. Insulin and secretagogue users should consider fasting alcohol intake and hypoglycemia later, including the next day. There is no health reason for a nondrinker to start. Discuss alcohol, monitoring and hypoglycemia plans, and ask for smoking cessation support.

title: One change this week
text: Glucose is not a personal grade. Recording meals, medicines, activity and sleep helps you discuss changes at visits. Persistent low mood, anxiety or diabetes distress deserves support. Choose one small action and one question for your next appointment.

title: Why activity helps
chapter: Start walking and strength exercise safely
text: Muscle contraction supports glucose uptake through pathways partly separate from insulin signaling. Regular activity improves insulin sensitivity, fitness and function. Exercise complements food and medication; glucose does not always fall immediately.

title: Weekly goals and a starting dose
chapter: Start walking and strength exercise safely
text: Many adults are advised to aim for at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly and strength exercise on 2–3 nonconsecutive days. Spread aerobic activity over at least three days, with no more than two consecutive inactive days. Begin above your current activity level even if below the target. Try ten minutes of comfortable walking after a meal, and interrupt long sitting about every 30 minutes.

title: Strength exercise at home
chapter: Start walking and strength exercise safely
text: Choose safe movements such as chair sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, band rows or supported heel raises. Begin with few repetitions and sets, then increase once the movement is stable. Breathe normally and use a stable chair. Discuss weight-bearing exercise with an active foot ulcer, and strenuous or straining exercise with proliferative retinopathy. Swimming is not automatically safe for an open foot wound.

title: Prepare according to medication risk
chapter: Start walking and strength exercise safely
text: Insulin, sulfonylurea and meglitinide users should consider glucose before and after activity and delayed hypoglycemia. Pre-exercise carbohydrate needs depend on glucose, active insulin and activity duration. One threshold does not fit everyone. Carry rapid glucose and agree on a monitoring plan for new activity. Stop and seek help for chest pain, severe dizziness or breathing difficulty. Do not try to force glucose down through exercise when unwell with high glucose and ketones.

title: Low glucose: when awake
chapter: Low glucose, sick days and monitoring
text: Treat glucose below 70 mg/dL as hypoglycemia. An adult who is awake and can swallow can take about 15 g of rapid glucose and recheck after 15 minutes. Repeat if still low. Use the product label to identify 15 g in glucose tablets or gel. With acarbose, use glucose rather than table sugar. Chocolate and high-fat snacks are slower to absorb. One yogurt or a fixed number of candies does not always provide 15 g.

title: Impaired consciousness or seizure is an emergency
chapter: Low glucose, sick days and monitoring
text: Do not give food or drink to someone unconscious or unable to swallow safely. Call emergency services; use prescribed glucagon if available and you have been trained. Severe hypoglycemia means assistance is needed, regardless of the measured glucose. Share emergency contacts, glucose location and glucagon instructions with family.

title: Sick days and ketoacidosis
chapter: Low glucose, sick days and monitoring
text: Vomiting, dehydration or fasting requires a medicine-specific plan. SGLT2 users can develop ketoacidosis without very high glucose. Severe vomiting, abdominal pain, rapid deep breathing or altered consciousness needs prompt assessment; do not wait based on glucose alone. A person with fluid restriction should not be told to drink unlimited water. Plans for type 1 insulin, SGLT2 medicines and metformin differ.

title: Monitoring, follow-up and visit questions
chapter: Low glucose, sick days and monitoring
text: Wash and dry hands before testing. Count after-meal time from the start of the meal. To convert mg/dL to mmol/L, divide by about 18. Home readings alone do not establish a diagnosis. HbA1c is usually reviewed every 3–6 months depending on goals and treatment changes. In type 2, kidney function, urine albumin, eyes and feet are assessed from diagnosis with follow-up adjusted to findings. Blood pressure and lipid targets also depend on cardiovascular risk. Ask: What are my targets? What if glucose goes low? What if I cannot eat? Can I take a new medicine or supplement with these?

title: Why can wounds go unnoticed?
chapter: Feet and complications: notice small warning signs
text: Diabetic neuropathy can cause tingling and burning, but also loss of sensation. Poor circulation can make wounds harder to heal. A painless wound is not necessarily safe.

title: Daily foot checks
chapter: Feet and complications: notice small warning signs
text: Check the tops, soles and between toes for blisters, wounds, redness and swelling. Use a mirror or family help. Wash in lukewarm water, dry between toes, and check inside well-fitting shoes before putting them on. Avoid barefoot walking; do not cut or chemically remove corns or calluses yourself. Hot packs or hot foot baths can burn feet with reduced sensation.

title: When to seek care
chapter: Feet and complications: notice small warning signs
text: Report a new wound, blister, redness, warmth, swelling or drainage promptly. Fever, spreading redness, black discoloration or a very cold or discolored foot requires urgent assessment. Do not delay because it is painless.

title: Eyes, kidneys and heart matter too
chapter: Feet and complications: notice small warning signs
text: Eye and kidney complications can be silent early, so follow-up testing matters. Manage glucose, blood pressure, lipids, smoking and appropriate medicines together. Tingling can also have causes such as B12 deficiency and needs assessment.

title: Quality and applicability, not just study count
text: A meta-analysis can include small, biased or short studies. A change in glucose does not prove prevention of complications. Trial formulations and doses may differ from products sold. Routine supplements for glucose management are not generally recommended.

title: Correcting deficiency is different from treating glucose
text: Long-term metformin use is associated with lower B12. Discuss testing with anemia, tingling or prolonged use. B12, vitamin D or magnesium supplementation should consider deficiency and individual factors; glucose improvement is not guaranteed for everyone. Some minerals can accumulate with impaired kidney function. Avoid stacking products without assessment.

title: Alpha-lipoic acid: limited long-term benefit
text: Short-term symptom findings should be separated from long-term benefit. A 2024 Cochrane review found probably little or no improvement in neuropathy symptoms after six months or more. It should not be presented as proven nerve protection.

title: Berberine, cinnamon, banaba and omega-3
text: Even with glucose-lowering studies, certainty, product quality and interactions need separate review. Berberine and similar supplements should not replace diabetes medicines. Cardiovascular findings for specific prescription products are not the same as findings for ordinary omega-3 supplements. Bring product, ingredient and strength details to visits; avoid advertisements promising cures or stopping medication.

title: Remember these
chapter: Diabetes: what happens inside the body?
text: Blood glucose is the amount of glucose in your blood. Insulin helps the body use glucose. Diagnostic thresholds (fasting glucose 126 mg/dL or higher, HbA1c 6.5% or higher) are not your personal target. Set your target with your care team. Write down whether each test was fasting, after a meal or an oral glucose tolerance test.

title: Remember these
text: Prediabetes is a chance to act. Not everyone with prediabetes develops diabetes. If you are overweight, work gradually toward losing 5–7% of your weight and about 150 minutes of activity such as walking each week. Have your glucose checked at least once a year.

title: Remember these
text: Take a photo of your medicine bag or prescription, and check the ingredient names next to the product names. Before starting cold medicine, painkillers, herbal remedies or supplements, tell the pharmacist that you take diabetes medicine. Do not stop or change medicines yourself when readings improve or when you cannot eat. Ask your care team or pharmacist for a plan in advance.

title: Remember these
chapter: Food: what and how much to eat?
text: You do not need to give up rice or noodles. Start with a plate that is half non-starchy vegetables, one quarter protein and one quarter rice or noodles. Cut down on sugary drinks and fruit juice; eat whole fruit in suitable portions. Before making big changes to what you eat, agree on medicine and glucose-checking plans with your care team.

title: Remember these
text: Keep regular sleep, such as waking at the same time each day. Mention loud snoring or daytime sleepiness at your visit. Alcohol can cause low glucose as late as the next day. If you use medicines that can cause low glucose (such as insulin or sulfonylureas), do not drink on an empty stomach. Glucose is not a grade. Choose one small action for this week, and ask for help to quit smoking if needed.

title: Remember these
chapter: Start walking and strength exercise safely
text: Start with a comfortable ten-minute walk after meals, and get up briefly about every 30 minutes when sitting for long periods. The goal is 150 minutes of moderate activity and strength exercise 2–3 times a week. Increase little by little from where you are now. If you use medicines that can cause low glucose, carry rapid glucose. Stop right away if you have chest pain, severe dizziness or trouble breathing.

title: Remember these
chapter: Low glucose, sick days and monitoring
text: If glucose is below 70 mg/dL and the person is awake and can swallow, take about 15 g of rapid glucose and recheck after 15 minutes. Repeat if still low. If the person is unconscious or cannot swallow, give nothing by mouth and call emergency services right away (119 in Korea, 115 in Vietnam). With severe vomiting, abdominal pain or fast breathing, get care promptly; do not wait based on the glucose number alone.

title: Remember these
chapter: Feet and complications: notice small warning signs
text: Check the tops, soles and between the toes every day. Use a mirror or ask family to help with the soles. Even if it does not hurt, get a new wound, blister, redness or swelling checked promptly. Do not walk barefoot, and avoid hot packs, hot foot baths and removing corns or calluses yourself.

title: Remember these
text: Supplements do not replace diabetes medicines. Avoid advertisements that promise a cure or say you can stop your medicines. Show the ingredients and strengths of products you take or plan to take at your visit, especially if you have kidney problems.

title: Metformin · biguanide
text: Primarily reduces excessive glucose production by the liver. Lowers glucose with low hypoglycemia risk alone and little weight gain. Diarrhea, nausea and abdominal discomfort. Rare lactic acidosis; severe kidney impairment, hypoxia or dehydration warrants particular assessment. Follow formulation-specific instructions. Review B12 and plans for contrast, surgery or dehydration.

title: DPP-4 inhibitor
text: Slows incretin breakdown, supporting glucose-dependent insulin release. Improves glucose, usually weight-neutral, low hypoglycemia risk alone. Headache or upper respiratory symptoms are reported with some ingredients; frequencies vary. Warnings include pancreatitis, severe joint pain and bullous pemphigoid. Heart failure cautions differ by ingredient. Many ingredients need dose review with kidney impairment. Linagliptin generally does not require renal dose adjustment.

title: SGLT2 inhibitor
text: Reduces kidney glucose reabsorption so glucose is excreted in urine. Helps glucose and weight; selected ingredients have proven heart failure and kidney outcome benefits. Genital fungal infections and increased urination; consider dehydration and low blood pressure. Urinary and genital infections differ. Rare ketoacidosis can occur without very high glucose. Severe infection symptoms also need prompt assessment. Discuss a plan for prolonged fasting, extreme carbohydrate restriction, dehydration or surgery. Respect prescribed fluid limits.

title: Sulfonylurea
text: Stimulates pancreatic beta cells to release insulin. Effective glucose lowering and relatively low cost. Hypoglycemia and weight gain. Severe or prolonged hypoglycemia, especially with older age, kidney impairment or poor intake. Review plans for skipped meals, more exercise or alcohol. Risk differs across ingredients.

title: Meglitinide · glinide
text: Promotes short-acting insulin release around meals. Primarily lowers post-meal glucose. Hypoglycemia and weight gain. Severe hypoglycemia. Repaglinide has important interactions with some other medicines. Check your prescribed instructions for missed meals; do not substitute another medicine yourself.

title: Thiazolidinedione · TZD
text: Improves insulin sensitivity through PPAR-gamma signaling. Improves insulin resistance with low hypoglycemia risk alone. Weight gain and edema. Worsening heart failure and fracture risk. Review ingredient-specific bladder cancer warnings for pioglitazone. Report rapid weight gain, leg swelling or breathlessness. Effects can develop gradually.

title: Alpha-glucosidase inhibitor
text: Slows intestinal carbohydrate digestion to reduce post-meal glucose rises. Improves post-meal glucose with low hypoglycemia risk alone. Gas, bloating and diarrhea. Ingredient-specific liver and intestinal cautions apply. Use glucose to treat combination-related hypoglycemia. Check meal-related instructions for the product. With acarbose or miglitol, use glucose, not table sugar, for hypoglycemia.

title: GLP-1 receptor agonist
text: Supports glucose-dependent insulin secretion and affects glucagon, appetite and gastric emptying. Improves glucose and weight. Heart and kidney benefits depend on the ingredient and studied population. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation. Review pancreatitis, gallbladder and dehydration cautions. Medullary thyroid cancer/MEN2 contraindications are product-specific. Report severe persistent abdominal pain or vomiting. Inform anesthesia teams and check special instructions for oral formulations.

title: Dual GIP/GLP-1 agonist
text: Acts on GIP and GLP-1 receptors to affect glucose regulation, appetite and weight. Tirzepatide improves glucose and weight; results depend on population, dose and comparator. Nausea, vomiting, diarrhea or constipation. Review pancreatitis, gallbladder and dehydration warnings and the product’s medullary thyroid cancer/MEN2 contraindications. Monitor digestive symptoms and reduced intake; ask about oral contraceptives, surgery and anesthesia.

title: Insulin
text: Replaces insufficient insulin to regulate glucose uptake and liver production. Essential in type 1 and effective when needed in type 2. Hypoglycemia, weight gain and injection-site reactions. Severe hypoglycemia. Confusing ingredients, concentrations or pens can be dangerous. Rotate injection sites and learn meal, exercise and sick-day plans. Do not interchange basal, mealtime or mixed formulations yourself.

title: Human insulin: confirm the formulation
text: This name alone cannot distinguish regular, NPH or mixed formulations. Only general insulin information is shown. Confirm the product, formulation and concentration with a pharmacist. Do not infer timing or duration from this result.

title: Miglitol: use glucose for hypoglycemia
text: Prepare for hypoglycemia when miglitol is combined with insulin or secretagogues. Sucrose digestion is delayed: use glucose tablets or gel if awake and able to swallow. Do not give anything by mouth if unconscious or unable to swallow; call emergency services.

title: Semaglutide: eyes and formulation
text: Injectable semaglutide labeling includes a retinopathy complication warning. Review existing retinopathy and rapid glucose improvement, and report vision changes. Injectable and oral instructions and indications differ.

title: Alogliptin: review heart failure risk
text: The US label calls for benefit-risk review and symptom monitoring in people at risk of heart failure. Share any heart failure or kidney impairment history.

title: Some ingredients are unverified
text: Results cover recognized ingredients only. No result does not mean safe. Check exact ingredient names on your prescription.

title: Repeated ingredient
text: This may be repeated input or the same ingredient in several products. Ask a pharmacist to check duplication. Planned use of different insulins is a different situation.

title: Medicines requiring hypoglycemia preparation
text: Insulin, sulfonylurea or glinide is present. Reduced meals, activity and alcohol change risk; other glucose-lowering medicines can increase it. Review monitoring and rapid glucose plans.

title: Review an incretin combination
text: Combining a DPP-4 inhibitor with GLP-1 or GIP/GLP-1 therapy is generally not recommended because added benefit is limited. Check the prescription intent; do not stop it yourself.

title: Use glucose for low blood sugar
text: Acarbose with insulin or secretagogues can cause hypoglycemia. Since acarbose delays sucrose digestion, use glucose tablets or gel. Do not feed an unconscious person; call emergency services.

title: Several ingredients in one class
text: Several ingredients share a class. Check whether the combination is intentional or duplicative. This flag does not establish a prescribing error.

title: Insulin plus TZD: review edema and heart failure
text: Review fluid retention and heart failure risk with this combination. Report sudden weight gain, leg swelling or breathlessness.

title: Repaglinide + gemfibrozil
text: The US label contraindicates this combination due to severe hypoglycemia concerns. Promptly confirm it with your prescriber or pharmacist. This tool does not set discontinuation or dose changes.

title: Repaglinide + clopidogrel
text: The US label advises avoiding this combination. Increased exposure and hypoglycemia risk require clinician review.

title: Saxagliptin: heart failure warning
text: People at elevated heart failure risk need individualized benefit-risk review. Report breathlessness, edema or rapid weight gain. Do not interpret this as equal risk for all DPP-4 ingredients.

title: Kidney function review
text: Kidney function changes risk or dosing for metformin, some DPP-4 medicines, insulin and secretagogues. Clinicians should review eGFR and product labels. This tool does not calculate doses.

title: Review a heart failure history
text: Review fluid retention and heart failure worsening with TZDs. SGLT2 benefit and fluid or blood pressure plans depend on ingredient and condition.

title: Fasting, dehydration and ketoacidosis plan
text: An SGLT2 ingredient is present. Agree in advance on surgery, fasting and serious illness plans. Severe vomiting, abdominal pain or rapid breathing needs prompt assessment even without very high glucose.

title: DPP · Knowler et al. (2002)
text: In high-risk adults, an intensive lifestyle program reduced diabetes incidence by 58% relative to placebo; metformin reduced it by 31%. This was a structured program in a high-risk population, not an individual absolute risk reduction or the effect of ordinary walking.

title: EMPA-KIDNEY Collaborative Group (2023)
text: In chronic kidney disease, empagliflozin lowered the composite risk of kidney disease progression or cardiovascular death compared with placebo. Participants met specific kidney and risk criteria. This does not imply the same effect for every SGLT2 ingredient or every person.

title: EMPA-KIDNEY Collaborative Group (2023)
text: In chronic kidney disease, empagliflozin lowered the composite risk of kidney disease progression or cardiovascular death compared with placebo. Participants met specific kidney and risk criteria. This does not imply the same effect for every SGLT2 ingredient or every person.

title: LEADER · Marso et al. (2016)
text: Liraglutide reduced major cardiovascular events versus placebo in people with type 2 diabetes at high cardiovascular risk. The finding concerns liraglutide and a high-risk population. Glucose lowering alone does not establish cardiovascular benefit for every medicine.

title: SURPASS-2 · Frías et al. (2021)
text: In a 40-week comparison in metformin-treated type 2 diabetes, tirzepatide reduced HbA1c and weight more than semaglutide 1 mg. This compares specific doses and duration; it does not prove superiority to every semaglutide dose or superiority for cardiovascular outcomes.
